subject: Vectorising looping through an adjacency matrix for speed-up

messages.author: 9cf7d6efe5c052b5
messages.subject: Vectorising looping through an adjacency matrix for speed-up
parts:
Dear all,

I am using Stan for statistical interference on networks. This works well but is fairly slow. Main reason is that I have to loop through all matrix elements (in fact only the upper triangular part). This process is not vectorised and I assume it would be much faster if I could transform my problem so that this would be possible. The general problem is that the connection probability for each matrix entry depends on the entry in another vector x (to be more precise the connection probability of A[i][j] depends on the distance between x[i] and x[j])
Below is a minimal working example. If you have any advice how to speed it up it would be much appreciated!

In general, is there anybody who used Stan for network analysis? Surprisingly, I didn't find any examples but it seems very well suited for it.

All the best,
Flo

interference_space = """
data {
    int<lower=0> n; // number of nodes
    int  A[n, n]; // adjacency matrix
}
parameters {
    real<lower=0.0, upper=1.0> p0; //base density
    real<lower=0.0, upper=100.0> p1; //distance dependent density
    real<lower=0.0, upper=100.0> p2; //distance dependency exponent   
    vector<lower=0.0, upper=1.0>[2] x[n]; // location in 2 dimensions 
}
model {
    for (i in 1:n)
        for (j in (i+1):n)
          A[i][j] ~ poisson( p0+p1*exp(-p2*(dot_self(x[i] - x[j])))) ;
}
"""

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: Vectorising looping through an adjacency matrix for speed-up
parts:
On Saturday, December 10, 2016 at 2:00:20 PM UTC-5, Florian Klimm wrote:
I am using Stan for statistical interference on networks. This works well but is fairly slow. Main reason is that I have to loop through all matrix elements (in fact only the upper triangular part). This process is not vectorised and I assume it would be much faster if I could transform my problem so that this would be possible.

That is not quite a correct assumption. The slowness is (in part) due to having sampling statements in the loop, which trigger a lot of memory allocations. Do this instead:

data {
  int<lower=1> n;
  int A[n,n];
}
transformed data {
  int n_choose_2;
  int A_lower[n * (n - 1) / 2]; // ignore integer division warnings
  n_choose_2 = n * (n - 1) / 2;
  {
    int pos;
    pos = 1;
    for (i in 1:n) for (j in (i + 1):n) {
      A_lower[pos] = A[i,j];
      pos = pos + 1;
    }
  }
}
model {
  vector[n_choose_2] lambda;
  int pos;
  pos = 1;
  for (i in 1:n) for (j in (i + 1):n) {
    lambda[pos] = p0 + p1 * exp(-p2 * dot_self(x[i] - x[j]));
    pos = pos + 1;
  }
  A_lower ~ poisson(lambda);
}

You would also probably be better off if you could change things around to use the poisson_log PMF instead of poisson.

Ben

Absolutely. That's what log_sum_exp is for :-)

log_lambda[pos] = log_sum_exp(log(p0), log(p1) - p2 * dot_self(x[i] - x[j]));

A_lower ~ poisson_log(log_lambda);

And Ben just added a choose function and I'm going to work on ++pos
and pos++, so this code can get a lot cleaner and without integer
division warnings.

- Bob
